column1: The first models examined in this chapter are ones in which real resources and money are used to produce transaction services, with these services being required to purchase consumption goods. These real resources can take the form of either time or goods. Most of this chapter, however, is devoted to the study of models that 1. Jovanovic (1982) and D. Romer (1986) embedded the Baumol-Tobin model in general equilibrium frameworks. impose a rigid restriction on the nature of transactions. Rather than allowing substitutability between time and money in carrying out transactions, cash-in-advance (CIA) models simply require that money balances be held to finance certain types of purchases; without money, these purchases cannot be made. CIA models, like MIU models, assume that money is special; unlike other financial assets, it either yields direct utility and therefore belongs in the utility function, or it has unique properties that allow it to be used to facilitate transactions. This chapter concludes with a look at some recent work based on search theory to explain how the nature of transactions gives rise to money.
